subChunks.title: Psychodynamic Therapy: Theory, Process & Evidence
subChunks.hookHtml: Freud's consulting room in Vienna, late 19th century: a woman lies on a couch and speaks freely about whatever comes to mind — without censorship, without direction. This is the 'talking cure', the founding method of psychoanalysis. More than 120 years later, psychodynamic therapies remain widely practised despite occupying an awkward position in evidence-based psychology: richly theorised, clinically sophisticated, and yet historically resistant to the kind of manualisation and randomised testing that CBT pioneered. The picture has changed substantially in the past two decades. Short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy (STPP) now has a credible RCT evidence base, long-term psychodynamic therapy shows efficacy for complex presentations where brief treatments fail, and psychodynamic ideas — the importance of early relationships, unconscious processes, the therapeutic relationship as a vehicle of change — have been substantially validated by attachment research and interpersonal neuroscience. Understanding psychodynamic approaches is not optional for an applied psychologist, even if they never practise within this tradition.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Core Psychodynamic Concepts

The unconscious: Psychodynamic approaches share the core assumption that much of mental life — including motivations, desires, fears, and conflicts — operates outside conscious awareness. Behaviour that appears self-defeating or inexplicable often reflects unconscious processes that served adaptive functions in the past but are no longer appropriate. Modern neuroscience provides partial support: extensive evidence for implicit memory, procedural emotional learning, and automatic affective processing demonstrates that behaviour is influenced by non-conscious systems.

Defence mechanisms: Ego defences are unconscious strategies that protect against anxiety produced by threatening impulses or information. Examples:

Repression       — keeping threatening thoughts/memories out of awareness
Projection       — attributing one's own unacceptable impulses to others
Rationalisation  — giving acceptable reasons for unacceptable behaviour
Sublimation      — channelling unacceptable impulses into socially valued activity
Reaction formation — acting opposite to one's actual impulse
Dissociation     — detachment from emotional content of experience

Defence mechanisms can be adaptive (sublimation, humour) or maladaptive (splitting, projective identification in severe personality pathology).

The Therapeutic Relationship as the Vehicle of Change

Transference: The unconscious displacement of feelings, expectations, and relational patterns from past relationships onto the therapist. A client who experienced an intrusive, critical parent may come to experience the therapist as critical and intrusive — even when no such behaviour has occurred. Transference is not a resistance to therapy; it is the medium through which past relational patterns become available for examination and modification.

Countertransference: The therapist's emotional response to the client — including both personal reactions stemming from the therapist's own history and induced emotional states that reflect the client's projected material. Modern psychodynamic practice treats countertransference as a clinical instrument: the therapist's internal experience provides data about the client's unconscious communication.

The therapeutic alliance in psychodynamic work: The early attachment literature (Bowlby) and subsequent research on the alliance demonstrate that the quality of the therapeutic relationship predicts outcome more strongly than any specific technique across all therapy modalities. In psychodynamic work, the relationship is not just a 'vehicle' — it is the primary site of curative change.

Short-Term Psychodynamic Psychotherapy (STPP)

STPP (Malan, 1976; Davanloo, 1980; Luborsky's Supportive-Expressive Therapy) applies psychodynamic principles within a focused, time-limited frame (12–40 sessions). A focus is negotiated with the client — typically a core conflictual relationship theme that underlies their presenting difficulties. Techniques include exploration of the therapeutic relationship, linking present difficulties to past experiences (the 'triangle of persons'), and interpretive work on defence and impulse.

Meta-analyses (Abbass et al., 2014) find STPP significantly superior to control conditions for depression, anxiety, somatic disorders, and personality disorders, with effect sizes comparable to CBT for many presentations. Long-term psychodynamic therapy (LTPP, >40 sessions) shows superior outcomes to shorter treatments for complex, severe, and comorbid presentations — an area where brief CBT often fails.

Person-Centred Therapy (Carl Rogers)

Carl Rogers (1951, 1961) proposed that psychological growth is natural and will occur in the right therapeutic conditions. The therapist's task is to provide three core conditions:

  • Unconditional positive regard: Accepting the client fully and non-judgementally — including aspects they find shameful or unacceptable — without making the relationship conditional on behavioural change.
  • Empathic understanding: Accurately sensing and communicating understanding of the client's inner world, as if from inside their perspective (not sympathy, which is an external response).
  • Congruence (authenticity): The therapist being genuine and transparent in the relationship — not hiding behind a professional role. Transparency about genuine reactions (when clinically appropriate) is preferred to therapeutic neutrality.

Rogers' research demonstrated that these conditions were both necessary and sufficient for therapeutic change — a claim that remains contested but has generated robust evidence that all three conditions predict positive outcome across therapy types. Person-centred therapy has a smaller RCT evidence base than CBT but is widely practised, particularly in counselling and primary care settings.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen begins this session with an unusual question: 'Can you think of a time when you found yourself repeating a pattern — maybe the same kind of relationship difficulty, or the same kind of conflict at work — that you didn't intend to repeat and didn't fully understand?' The room is thoughtful.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: That repetition — that compulsion to repeat — is what psychodynamic theory is trying to explain. Not in terms of habits or conditioning (though those matter), but in terms of something more like a template: a set of expectations about relationships that was formed very early, never consciously examined, and that keeps getting played out in new settings. The consulting room makes that template visible.

storyBeats.speaker: Transference in action
storyBeats.text: A client with a history of abandonment repeatedly arrived late for sessions and then accused the therapist of 'not really caring' when the therapist ended sessions on time despite the late arrival. The therapist — rather than simply explaining the time boundary — recognised that the client was unconsciously recreating the experience of abandonment: arriving late (ensuring rejection) to confirm the expectation that caring people ultimately leave. This recognition, and the gentle naming of the pattern in the here-and-now of the therapeutic relationship, became the most therapeutically powerful moment of the treatment.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: Rogers' insight is deceptively simple. He said: people don't change because we confront their errors, analyse their defences, or give them homework. They change when they experience being truly understood and unconditionally accepted — perhaps for the first time. The conditions he described are not soft skills. Genuine unconditional positive regard in the presence of someone you disagree with is one of the hardest things a human being can do.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
A 40-year-old client, David, has been in psychodynamic therapy for 6 sessions for longstanding depression and relationship difficulties. He describes a pattern of intense friendships that end when he perceives the other person as becoming 'too controlling'. In the most recent session, he arrived 15 minutes late and said: 'I nearly didn't come. You're always pointing out what I'm doing wrong, just like everyone else.'

  1. Identify the clinical concept illustrated by David's comment about his therapist and explain it.
  2. How might the psychodynamic therapist respond to David's statement in a way that uses this moment therapeutically, rather than simply correcting the misperception?
  3. How does psychodynamic therapy understand the origin of David's pattern of brief intense friendships that end over perceived control?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. David's comment illustrates transference: he is unconsciously displacing feelings and expectations from past relationships (where he experienced criticism and control) onto the therapist, perceiving criticism and control that may not be present in the therapeutic relationship. This is not simply 'resistance' or 'distortion' — it is the past relational template actively operating in the present relationship with the therapist. The therapeutic value is that this pattern, which David reports experiencing in his friendships, is now visible and available for examination in the here-and-now of the session.

2. A therapeutically useful psychodynamic response might be: 'I notice that something has shifted between us in the last few minutes — you came in late, and now you're telling me I'm like everyone else who has criticised you. I'm wondering if this moment here — something in this room, or in the space between us — might feel like it's confirming something that's been painful to confirm many times before. Can we slow down and stay with that feeling together, rather than moving past it?' This response: (a) doesn't immediately correct David's perception (which would miss the therapeutic opportunity); (b) acknowledges the interpersonal moment in the room (the here-and-now); (c) links it gently to the broader pattern without interpreting it as definitively symbolic; and (d) invites collaborative exploration rather than asserting the therapist's interpretation.

3. Psychodynamic theory would understand David's pattern of brief friendships as reflecting an early relational template — likely from attachment experiences in childhood — in which closeness carries the implicit expectation of control, loss of autonomy, or criticism. The pattern of seeking intense connection followed by withdrawal when control is perceived may reflect an anxious or avoidant attachment style, with 'control' functioning as a signal for anticipated rejection or engulfment. The compulsion to repeat this pattern reflects the internal working model (Bowlby) operating below conscious awareness: David is not choosing to sabotage friendships — he is enacting a deeply held relational schema. The psychodynamic work involves making this schema conscious and available for modification through the corrective emotional experience of the therapeutic relationship — where the therapist's response to David's 'control' perception is neither the anticipated criticism nor withdrawal.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Some CBT practitioners argue that psychodynamic therapy's focus on the therapeutic relationship and unconscious processes is both theoretically unscientific and empirically less supported than CBT. Evaluate this critique, drawing on contemporary evidence for psychodynamic therapies and considering what psychodynamic theory contributes to psychological practice that CBT may not fully capture. Aim for 200–250 words.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The claim that psychodynamic therapy lacks scientific support was more defensible 30 years ago than today. Contemporary meta-analyses (Abbass et al., 2014; Driessen et al., 2015) provide robust evidence for short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy (STPP) across depression, anxiety, and somatic disorders, with effect sizes comparable to CBT for many conditions. Long-term psychodynamic therapy (LTPP) shows particular advantages over brief treatments for complex, severe, and comorbid presentations — a clinically important population where brief CBT often fails or requires repeated courses.

The accusation of theoretical unscientificity has more nuance. Specific Freudian claims (e.g., psychosexual stage theory, penis envy) do not meet scientific standards. However, the broader psychodynamic framework — the importance of early relational experiences, unconscious affective processes, the role of the therapeutic relationship, and the compulsion to repeat relational patterns — has substantial empirical support from attachment research, affective neuroscience, and interpersonal process research. The unconscious is no longer a theoretical construct — it is a robust empirical finding.

Psychodynamic theory contributes perspectives that CBT does not fully capture. The depth and complexity of personality pathology — particularly in borderline and narcissistic presentations — requires relational and developmental understanding that symptom-focused approaches may miss. Countertransference as a clinical instrument, the role of early trauma in shaping procedural relational memory, and the therapeutic relationship as a vehicle of change rather than merely its medium all reflect psychodynamic insights that have influenced even contemporary CBT developments (schema therapy, DBT, ISTDP). A thoughtful clinician will draw on both traditions.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what the psychodynamic idea of 'transference' means — give them a concrete, relatable example of how someone might bring patterns from past relationships into a new one without realising it.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The therapist's emotional responses to the client — including both reactions from the therapist's own history and induced emotional states reflecting the client's projected material. Modern psychodynamic practice treats this as a clinical instrument.

Alexander's (1946) concept that therapeutic change occurs when the client has a fundamentally different relational experience in therapy than they had in the formative relationships that shaped their difficulties — e.g., experiencing non-judgement after a history of critical caregiving.

The capacity to understand behaviour in terms of mental states — to reflect on one's own and others' thoughts, feelings, desires, and intentions. Developed in the attachment relationship; impaired in borderline personality disorder. Fonagy's Mentalisation-Based Treatment (MBT) targets this capacity.

Rogers' core therapeutic condition: accepting the client fully and without conditions — not withdrawing warmth or acceptance when the client reveals aspects of themselves that might be judged negatively. Empirically predicts therapeutic outcome across modalities.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following best defines 'transference' in psychodynamic therapy?
options: The therapist's emotional reaction to the client, which can be used as clinical data
The unconscious displacement of feelings and relational expectations from past relationships onto the therapist
The client's conscious attempt to change the subject when therapy becomes uncomfortable
The transfer of skills learned in therapy to everyday life
questions.correctAnswer: The unconscious displacement of feelings and relational expectations from past relationships onto the therapist
questions.explanationHtml: Transference is the unconscious process by which feelings, expectations, and relational patterns from past significant relationships — typically with early caregivers — are displaced onto the therapist. The client experiences the therapist through the lens of past relationships, often without awareness that they are doing so. This is not deliberate distortion but an expression of the internal working model. In psychodynamic work, transference is therapeutically valuable — it makes past relational patterns available for examination in the present therapeutic relationship. Option A describes countertransference; option C describes avoidance or resistance; option D is a generalisation concept from other frameworks.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: Contemporary meta-analyses show that short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy (STPP) is significantly less effective than CBT for all psychological conditions.
questions.explanationHtml: False. Contemporary meta-analyses (Abbass et al., 2014; Driessen et al., 2015) find STPP significantly superior to control conditions with effect sizes comparable to those for CBT for many presentations, including depression, anxiety disorders, and somatic disorders. Head-to-head comparisons between STPP and CBT typically show no significant difference in outcome for mild-to-moderate presentations. Long-term psychodynamic therapy may outperform brief CBT for complex and severe presentations. The earlier dismissal of psychodynamic therapy as lacking evidence does not reflect the contemporary literature.

questions.questionHtml: Rogers proposed that unconditional positive regard, empathic understanding, and congruence are 'necessary and sufficient' conditions for therapeutic change. Which of the following most accurately represents the current evidence on this claim?
options: The claim has been fully validated — these three conditions are all that is needed for therapeutic change
The conditions have been discredited — specific techniques are necessary, and relationship factors are largely irrelevant
The conditions predict positive outcome across therapy types, but their sufficiency is debated; specific techniques also contribute to outcome for particular presentations
Only unconditional positive regard has empirical support; empathy and congruence have not been validated
questions.correctAnswer: The conditions predict positive outcome across therapy types, but their sufficiency is debated; specific techniques also contribute to outcome for particular presentations
questions.explanationHtml: Research consistently shows that all three Rogerian conditions (particularly empathy and unconditional positive regard) predict positive therapy outcome — this is part of the common factors evidence base. However, the sufficiency claim is not well-supported for all presentations: for specific phobias, OCD, and PTSD, evidence strongly suggests that specific techniques (ERP, trauma processing) are required over and above relationship factors. The consensus is that relationship factors are necessary but not always sufficient, and that both common factors and specific techniques contribute to outcome in ways that vary by presentation and severity.
